description: We are VITamins! Nandita Kale and Anvi Sharma from Vishwakarma Institute of Technology, Pune. Driven by curiosity and a shared interest in technology, we came together to explore an exciting challenge: making future Martian exploration smarter and safer. We believe in learning by building, thinking beyond conventional solutions, and turning ambitious ideas into something tangible. This journey has been all about collaboration, experimentation and quite literally reaching for the stars!!
summary: MARSCOPE (Martian Exploration & Survival Companion) is an intelligent, science-driven planetary exploration platform designed to transform how future astronauts navigate and investigate Mars. By integrating multi-mission NASA observations, including MOLA, THEMIS, HiRISE and CRISM, MARSCOPE creates an interactive scientific map of the Martian surface, revealing terrain characteristics, geological features, mineralogical evidence and potential hazards. Its terrain-aware, multi-objective route planner identifies optimal Marswalk paths by balancing astronaut safety, resource efficiency and scientific exploration opportunities. Going beyond conventional navigation, MARSCOPE incorporates an EVA mission simulator to estimate travel time, oxygen and power consumption, and return-to-base feasibility. An AI-powered scientific assistant further translates complex planetary data into actionable exploration insights. By unifying planetary GIS, intelligent route optimization and mission simulation, MARSCOPE bridges the gap between discovering Mars and planning its exploration—helping astronauts explore not just where they can go, but what they can discover and whether they can safely return.
details:
When we started working on MARSCOPE, we wanted to approach the challenge from the perspective of someone who might actually have to explore Mars. We realised that choosing a destination is only one part of the problem. The more difficult question is deciding how to get there while taking the surrounding conditions into account. That became the motivation behind our project.

The application allows users to interact with the Martian surface, select locations and experiment with different ways of travelling between them. Behind the interface, the backend processes geographical information and applies pathfinding logic to find a suitable route. We have used the A* algorithm for this because it allows us to evaluate possible paths rather than simply joining two locations with a straight line. This gives us a starting point for comparing routes based on factors such as distance, elevation and mapped hazards.

We see the main benefit of this approach in the way it brings several kinds of information together. A user does not have to look at a map in one place and separately interpret terrain information somewhere else. It also makes the decision-making process easier to understand, a route that looks convenient on a map may not necessarily be the most practical one to take.

For development, we chose Flutter and Dart for the frontend because they allowed us to build an interactive interface that could run on both mobile and web. We used Python and Flask for the backend, where we implemented the route-planning logic and created APIs to communicate with the application. We also worked with NASA's Mars data services to access map imagery and elevation layers. We did not require specialised hardware; the project was developed and tested using our computers, software tools and emulators.

The creative aspect of MARSCOPE lies in treating exploration as a decision-making problem rather than just a mapping exercise. We wanted users to be able to experiment with routes, compare alternatives and understand the reasoning behind a suggested path. It also creates opportunities to extend the application into areas such as mission resource planning and scientific site selection.

While making our decisions, we had to be careful about the accuracy of the information. Some of our current elevation estimates and hazard regions are approximations, so we distinguish these from verified scientific observations rather than presenting them as mission grade data.

Ultimately, we wanted to build a project that demonstrates how software can help make planetary exploration more systematic. MARSCOPE is an initial step towards that idea and we hope it can be developed further as more detailed Martian datasets and mission planning capabilities become available!
